Los perfiles lipídicos Los perfiles lipídicos constan de varios […]
content:
Como profesional de la medicina funcional, a menudo hago hincapié en la importancia de controlar los perfiles lipídicos a medida que las personas envejecen. Los perfiles lipídicos, que incluyen los niveles de colesterol y triglicéridos, son indicadores fundamentales de la salud cardiovascular y el bienestar general.

Los perfiles lipídicos

Los perfiles lipídicos constan de varios componentes, como el colesterol de lipoproteínas de baja densidad (LDL), el colesterol de lipoproteínas de alta densidad (HDL), los triglicéridos y el colesterol total. Estos lípidos desempeñan un papel importante en las funciones celulares y son componentes esenciales de las membranas celulares.

Perfiles lipídicos y envejecimiento

  • Cambios con el paso del tiempo: A medida que las personas envejecen, sus perfiles lipídicos suelen experimentar cambios significativos. El colesterol LDL tiende a aumentar, lo que puede conducir a la aterosclerosis si no se controla eficazmente. El colesterol HDL, conocido por sus efectos protectores contra las enfermedades cardiacas, puede disminuir (Heitmann et al., 1993).
  • Impacto en el envejecimiento celular: Los lípidos forman parte integral de la estructura y función celular. Un metabolismo anómalo de los lípidos puede provocar disfunción celular y promover el estrés oxidativo y la inflamación, que son fundamentales en el proceso de envejecimiento (Kaplon et al., 2014).

Perfiles lipídicos y enfermedades relacionadas con la edad

  • Enfermedades cardiovasculares: El colesterol LDL elevado y el colesterol HDL bajo están relacionados con un mayor riesgo de enfermedades cardiovasculares, que son comunes en los adultos mayores (Ferrara et al., 1997).
  • Trastornos neurodegenerativos: Estudios recientes han sugerido una relación entre la dislipidemia y el riesgo de desarrollar enfermedades neurodegenerativas como la enfermedad de Alzheimer, postulando que los desequilibrios lipídicos podrían influir en la patogénesis de la enfermedad (Solomon et al., 2009).

Estrategias para optimizar los perfiles lipídicos

  • Dieta: La incorporación de una dieta rica en ácidos grasos omega-3, fibra soluble y esteroles vegetales puede ayudar a mejorar los perfiles lipídicos.
  • Ejercicio: La actividad física regular puede aumentar el colesterol HDL y disminuir el colesterol LDL y los triglicéridos.
  • Medicación: Cuando los cambios en el estilo de vida son insuficientes, pueden recetarse medicamentos como las estatinas para ayudar a controlar los niveles de lípidos.

Futuras líneas de investigación

La investigación en curso continúa explorando las complejas relaciones entre los perfiles lipídicos, el envejecimiento y la longevidad. Las innovaciones en las terapias hipolipemiantes y la medicina personalizada son áreas prometedoras que podrían influir significativamente en la forma de gestionar el envejecimiento y los riesgos asociados.

Conocer y controlar los perfiles lipídicos es importante para envejecer de forma saludable y manejar los factores de riesgo asociados a las enfermedades relacionadas con la edad. El control periódico y la gestión proactiva de los lípidos pueden contribuir sustancialmente a aumentar la longevidad y mejorar la calidad de vida.

title: The Role of Lipid Profiles in Aging and Age-Related Diseases
excerpt: As a functional medicine practitioner, I often emphasize the importance of monitoring lipid profiles as individuals age. Lipid profiles, which include cholesterol and triglyceride levels, are critical indicators of cardiovascular health and overall well-being. This blog explores how changes in lipid profiles can influence aging and the development of age-related diseases, supported by the latest […]
content:
As a functional medicine practitioner, I often emphasize the importance of monitoring lipid profiles as individuals age. Lipid profiles, which include cholesterol and triglyceride levels, are critical indicators of cardiovascular health and overall well-being. This blog explores how changes in lipid profiles can influence aging and the development of age-related diseases, supported by the latest scientific literature.

Understanding Lipid Profiles

Lipid profiles consist of several components, including low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol, high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol, triglycerides, and total cholesterol. These lipids play significant roles in cellular functions and are essential components of cell membranes.

Lipid Profiles and Aging

  1. Changes Over Time: As people age, their lipid profiles typically undergo significant changes. LDL cholesterol tends to increase, which can lead to atherosclerosis if not managed effectively. HDL cholesterol, known for its protective effects against heart disease, can decrease (Heitmann et al., 1993).
  2. Impact on Cellular Aging: Lipids are integral to cellular structure and function. Abnormal lipid metabolism can lead to cellular dysfunction, promoting oxidative stress and inflammation, which are pivotal in the aging process (Kaplon et al., 2014).

Lipid Profiles and Age-Related Diseases

  • Cardiovascular Disease: Elevated LDL cholesterol and low HDL cholesterol are linked with an increased risk of cardiovascular diseases, which are common in older adults (Ferrara et al., 1997).
  • Neurodegenerative Disorders: Recent studies have suggested a link between dyslipidemia and the risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease, positing that lipid imbalances might influence the disease pathogenesis (Solomon et al., 2009).

Strategies to Optimize Lipid Profiles

  • Diet: Incorporating a diet high in omega-3 fatty acids, soluble fiber, and plant sterols can help improve lipid profiles.
  • Exercise: Regular physical activity can increase HDL cholesterol and decrease LDL cholesterol and triglycerides.
  • Medication: When lifestyle changes are insufficient, medications such as statins may be prescribed to help manage lipid levels.

Future Directions in Research

Ongoing research continues to explore the complex relationships between lipid profiles, aging, and longevity. Innovations in lipid-lowering therapies and personalized medicine are promising areas that could significantly impact how we manage aging and associated risks.

Understanding and managing lipid profiles is important for healthy aging and for managing risk factors associated with age-related disease. Regular monitoring and proactive management of lipids can substantially contribute to enhanced longevity and improved quality of life.

References

  • Heitmann, B. L., Erikson, H., Ellsinger, B. M., Mikkelsen, K. L., & Larsson, B. (1993). Mortality associated with body fat, fat-free mass and body mass index among 60-year-old Swedish men—a 22-year follow-up. The study of men born in 1913. Annals of Internal Medicine, 119(7 Pt 2), 669-673.
  • Kaplon, R. E., Gano, L. B., & Seals, D. R. (2014). Vascular endothelial function and oxidative stress are related to dietary niacin intake among healthy middle-aged and older adults. Journal of Applied Physiology, 116(1), 156-163.
  • Ferrara, A., Barrett-Connor, E., & Shan, J. (1997). Total, LDL, and HDL cholesterol decrease with age in older men and women. The Rancho Bernardo Study 1984-1994. Circulation, 96(1), 37-43.
  • Solomon, A., Kivipelto, M., Wolozin, B., Zhou, J., & Whitmer, R. A. (2009). Midlife serum cholesterol and increased risk of Alzheimer’s and vascular dementia three decades later. Dementia and geriatric cognitive disorders, 28(1), 75-80.

title: Semaglutida y pérdida de peso: cómo funciona y descubrimientos recientes
excerpt: Mientras la epidemia de obesidad sigue creciendo, tratamientos innovadores como la semaglutida ocupan los titulares por su potencial para ayudar a perder peso de forma significativa. Desarrollada originalmente para el tratamiento de la diabetes de tipo 2, la semaglutida ha mostrado resultados prometedores en el control de la obesidad. En este blog se analiza la […]
content:
Mientras la epidemia de obesidad sigue creciendo, tratamientos innovadores como la semaglutida ocupan los titulares por su potencial para ayudar a perder peso de forma significativa. Desarrollada originalmente para el tratamiento de la diabetes de tipo 2, la semaglutida ha mostrado resultados prometedores en el control de la obesidad. En este blog se analiza la eficacia de la semaglutida en la pérdida de peso, con el respaldo de las investigaciones más recientes.

¿Qué es la semaglutida?

La semaglutida es un agonista del receptor del GLP-1 (péptido similar al glucagón-1) que imita la hormona incretina, segregada de forma natural en respuesta a la ingesta de alimentos. Conocido comercialmente como Ozempic, Rybelsus y Wegovy, se administra mediante inyección o comprimido oral y fue aprobado inicialmente para el tratamiento de la diabetes de tipo 2. La semaglutida ha llamado la atención por su eficacia en el control de los niveles de azúcar en sangre y por sus importantes beneficios en la pérdida de peso, lo que llevó a su aprobación bajo la marca Wegovy para el tratamiento de la obesidad.

Mecanismos de acción

El principal mecanismo de acción de la semaglutida para ayudar a perder peso es su capacidad para regular el apetito y disminuir el apetito, lo que conduce a una reducción de la ingesta calórica. También ayuda a ralentizar el vaciado gástrico, lo que se traduce en un aumento más gradual de los niveles de azúcar en sangre después de las comidas. Además, la semaglutida estimula la secreción de insulina cuando los niveles de glucosa son elevados, lo que contribuye al control glucémico.

Investigaciones recientes sobre la pérdida de peso

Un estudio de referencia realizado por Wilding et al. (2021) en el New England Journal of Medicine demostró que los participantes que tomaban semaglutida perdían significativamente más peso que los que tomaban placebo. La pérdida media de peso fue de aproximadamente el 15% del peso corporal a lo largo de 68 semanas. Otras investigaciones de Davies et al. (2021) han demostrado que el uso a largo plazo de Semaglutida puede mantener la pérdida de peso, un factor crucial para el control de la obesidad.

Beneficios más allá de la pérdida de peso

Además de reducir el peso corporal, la semaglutida se ha asociado a otros beneficios para la salud. Entre ellos se incluyen mejoras en la salud cardiaca, como la reducción de los factores de riesgo de enfermedades cardiovasculares, por ejemplo la disminución de los niveles de colesterol LDL. Para las personas prediabéticas, la semaglutida también puede retrasar la aparición de la diabetes tipo 2.

Consideraciones y efectos secundarios

Aunque la semaglutida es un gran avance en el control del peso, entre los posibles efectos secundarios se incluyen problemas gastrointestinales como náuseas, vómitos, diarrea y estreñimiento, que suelen ser transitorios.

La semaglutida representa un avance significativo en el tratamiento de la obesidad y ofrece nuevas esperanzas a las personas que luchan por controlar su peso. A medida que avanza la investigación, las posibilidades de ampliar las aplicaciones de este fármaco al tratamiento de otros trastornos metabólicos siguen siendo prometedoras.

Importante: La semaglutida es un medicamento con receta. No es apropiada para todas las personas, tiene posibles efectos secundarios y contraindicaciones, y debe usarse únicamente bajo la supervisión de un médico con licencia. El tratamiento con receta se brinda solo cuando es médicamente apropiado, tras la evaluación de un profesional de salud con licencia, y los resultados individuales varían.

title: Semaglutide and Weight Loss: How It Works and Recent Findings
excerpt: As the obesity epidemic continues to grow, innovative treatments like Semaglutide are making headlines for their potential to aid significant weight loss. Originally developed for type 2 diabetes treatment, Semaglutide has shown promising results in obesity management. What is Semaglutide? Semaglutide is a GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonist that mimics the incretin hormone, which is […]
content:
As the obesity epidemic continues to grow, innovative treatments like Semaglutide are making headlines for their potential to aid significant weight loss. Originally developed for type 2 diabetes treatment, Semaglutide has shown promising results in obesity management.

What is Semaglutide?

Semaglutide is a GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) receptor agonist that mimics the incretin hormone, which is naturally secreted in response to food intake. Known commercially as Ozempic, Rybelsus, and Wegovy, it is administered via injection or oral tablet and was initially approved for the treatment of type 2 diabetes. Semaglutide has gained attention for its effectiveness in managing blood sugar levels and for its significant benefits in weight loss, which led to its approval under the brand name Wegovy for treating obesity.

Mechanisms of Action

Semaglutide’s primary mechanism for aiding weight loss is its ability to regulate appetite and decrease hunger, which leads to reduced caloric intake. It also helps slow down gastric emptying, resulting in a more gradual increase in blood sugar levels after meals. Additionally, Semaglutide stimulates insulin secretion when glucose levels are high, aiding in glycemic control.

Recent Research on Weight Loss

A landmark study by Wilding et al. (2021) in the New England Journal of Medicine demonstrated that participants using Semaglutide lost significantly more weight compared to those on placebo. The average weight loss was about 15% of body weight over 68 weeks. Further research by Davies et al. (2021) has shown that long-term use of Semaglutide can sustain weight loss, a crucial factor for obesity management.

Benefits Beyond Weight Loss

Beyond reducing body weight, Semaglutide has been associated with several other health benefits. These include improvements in cardiac health, such as reductions in risk factors for cardiovascular disease like lower LDL cholesterol levels. For pre-diabetic individuals, Semaglutide can also delay the onset of type 2’s.

Considerations and Side Effects

While Semaglutide is a breakthrough in weight management, potential side effects include gastrointestinal issues such as nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, and constipation, which are generally transient.

Semaglutide represents a significant advancement in the treatment of obesity, offering new hope for individuals struggling with weight management. As research continues, the potential for broader applications of this drug in treating other metabolic disorders remains promising.

References

  • Wilding, J. P. H., Batterham, R. L., Calanna, S., et al. (2021). Once-Weekly Semaglutide in Adults with Overweight or Obesity. New England Journal of Medicine, 384, 989-1002.
  • Davies, M., Faerch, L., Jeppesen, O. K., et al. (2021). Semaglutide 2.4 mg for the Treatment of Obesity: Key Elements of the STEP Trials 1 to 5. Obesity Reviews, 22, e13154.

Important: Semaglutide is a prescription medication. It is not appropriate for everyone, has potential side effects and contraindications, and should be used only under the supervision of a licensed clinician. Prescription treatment is provided only when medically appropriate following evaluation by a licensed healthcare professional, and individual results vary.

title: Estrés oxidativo y envejecimiento: comprender la conexión
excerpt: A medida que envejecemos, nuestros cuerpos sufren diversos cambios bioquímicos, y el estrés oxidativo desempeña un papel fundamental en el proceso de envejecimiento. Este blog profundiza en los mecanismos detrás del estrés oxidativo y su impacto en el envejecimiento, brindando información sobre cómo el manejo del estrés oxidativo puede potencialmente retardar el envejecimiento y mejorar […]
content:
A medida que envejecemos, nuestros cuerpos sufren diversos cambios bioquímicos, y el estrés oxidativo desempeña un papel fundamental en el proceso de envejecimiento. Este blog profundiza en los mecanismos detrás del estrés oxidativo y su impacto en el envejecimiento, brindando información sobre cómo el manejo del estrés oxidativo puede potencialmente retardar el envejecimiento y mejorar los resultados de salud.

Comprender el estrés oxidativo

El estrés oxidativo ocurre cuando hay un desequilibrio entre los radicales libres (moléculas inestables que pueden dañar las células) y los antioxidantes en el cuerpo. Los radicales libres se generan a través de procesos metabólicos normales, pero pueden acumularse en respuesta a factores ambientales como la contaminación, la radiación y la dieta. Cuando el cuerpo no puede neutralizar eficazmente estos radicales libres con antioxidantes, se produce estrés oxidativo.

El estrés oxidativo y su impacto en el envejecimiento

El estrés oxidativo contribuye al envejecimiento y al desarrollo de enfermedades relacionadas con la edad al dañar componentes celulares como el ADN, las proteínas y los lípidos. Este daño se acumula con el tiempo y provoca:

Senescencia celular: las células pierden su capacidad de funcionar y dividirse, contribuyendo al proceso de envejecimiento y al deterioro de la función de los órganos.

Inflamación: La inflamación crónica provocada por el estrés oxidativo es una vía común para muchas enfermedades relacionadas con la edad, como la artritis, la enfermedad de Alzheimer y las enfermedades cardiovasculares.

Disfunción mitocondrial: las mitocondrias, las fábricas de energía de las células, son particularmente susceptibles al daño oxidativo. La función mitocondrial deteriorada reduce la energía disponible para las células, lo que contribuye a la fatiga y la disminución de la capacidad física que se observan a menudo en el envejecimiento.

Estrategias para combatir el estrés oxidativo

Reducir el estrés oxidativo puede ser una estrategia clave para ralentizar el proceso de envejecimiento y reducir el riesgo de enfermedades:

Dieta rica en antioxidantes: el consumo de alimentos ricos en antioxidantes, como las vitaminas C y E, el betacaroteno y otros fitonutrientes, puede ayudar a equilibrar los radicales libres. Las frutas, verduras, nueces y semillas son fuentes excelentes.

Modificaciones del estilo de vida: evitar fumar, reducir la exposición a la contaminación y minimizar la exposición a la luz ultravioleta pueden disminuir la producción de radicales libres.

Ejercicio regular: el ejercicio mejora el sistema de defensa antioxidante del cuerpo y mejora la función mitocondrial, aunque es importante equilibrar la intensidad del ejercicio, ya que el ejercicio excesivo puede aumentar el estrés oxidativo.

Comprender el vínculo entre el estrés oxidativo y el envejecimiento proporciona información valiosa sobre cómo las elecciones de estilo de vida pueden influir en la tasa de envejecimiento y la aparición de enfermedades relacionadas con la edad. Al adoptar estrategias para reducir el estrés oxidativo, las personas pueden promover un envejecimiento más saludable y mejorar el bienestar general.

title: Oxidative Stress and Aging: Understanding the Connection

content:
As we age, our bodies undergo various biochemical changes, with oxidative stress playing a pivotal role in the aging process.

Understanding Oxidative Stress

Oxidative stress occurs when there’s an imbalance between free radicals (unstable molecules that can damage cells) and antioxidants in the body. Free radicals are generated through normal metabolic processes but can accumulate in response to environmental factors such as pollution, radiation, and diet. When the body cannot effectively neutralize these free radicals with antioxidants, it leads to oxidative stress.

Oxidative Stress and Its Impact on Aging

Oxidative stress contributes to aging and the development of age-related diseases by damaging cellular components such as DNA, proteins, and lipids. This damage accumulates over time, leading to:

  • Cellular Senescence: Cells lose their ability to function and divide, contributing to the aging process and the decline in organ function.
  • Inflammation: Chronic inflammation triggered by oxidative stress is a common pathway for many age-related diseases, including arthritis, Alzheimer’s disease, and cardiovascular disease.
  • Mitochondrial Dysfunction: Mitochondria, the energy factories of cells, are particularly susceptible to oxidative damage. Impaired mitochondrial function reduces the energy available to cells, contributing to the fatigue and decreased physical capacity often seen in aging.

Strategies to Combat Oxidative Stress

Reducing oxidative stress can be a key strategy in slowing the aging process and reducing the risk of disease:

  • Antioxidant-Rich Diet: Consuming foods high in antioxidants such as vitamins C and E, beta-carotene, and other phytonutrients can help balance free radicals. Fruits, vegetables, nuts, and seeds are excellent sources.
  • Lifestyle Modifications: Avoiding smoking, reducing exposure to pollution, and minimizing ultraviolet light exposure can decrease free radical production.
  • Regular Exercise: Exercise enhances the body’s antioxidant defense system and improves mitochondrial function, though it’s important to balance exercise intensity as excessive exercise can increase oxidative stress.

Understanding the link between oxidative stress and aging provides valuable insights into how lifestyle choices can influence the rate of aging and the onset of age-related diseases. By adopting strategies to reduce oxidative stress, individuals can promote healthier aging and enhance overall well-being.

title: La cronología del envejecimiento: Cuándo esperar los distintos síntomas del envejecimiento
excerpt: A menudo hablo del proceso natural de envejecimiento con mis pacientes. content:
A menudo hablo del proceso natural de envejecimiento con mis pacientes. Entender cuándo y por qué aparecen determinados síntomas del envejecimiento puede ayudarnos a prepararnos mejor y a gestionar estos cambios de forma proactiva. Esta guía ofrece una cronología general de los síntomas más comunes del envejecimiento y explica cómo pueden manifestarse a lo largo de la vida.

Entender los síntomas del envejecimiento

El envejecimiento es un proceso complejo en el que influyen la genética, el estilo de vida, el entorno y otros factores. Aunque cada persona envejece de forma diferente, existen ciertos patrones y síntomas comunes que tienden a aparecer en las distintas etapas de la vida.

Cronología general de los síntomas del envejecimiento

De los 30 a los 40 años

  • Niveles de energía: Muchos empiezan a notar una disminución de los niveles de energía.
  • Cambios en la piel: Aparecen los primeros signos de arrugas y piel menos elástica.
  • Ralentización metabólica: El metabolismo comienza a ralentizarse, lo que facilita el aumento de peso.
  • Masa muscular: Comienza la pérdida gradual de masa muscular.

De los 40 a los 50 años

  • Visión y audición: Pueden notarse ligeras disminuciones de la visión y la audición.
  • Salud articular: Puede empezar a notarse rigidez y molestias en las articulaciones, sobre todo si no se hace ejercicio con regularidad.
  • Cambios hormonales: Las mujeres entran en la perimenopausia que conduce a la menopausia, con síntomas como sofocos y cambios de humor. Los hombres pueden experimentar una disminución de los niveles de testosterona, lo que afecta al estado de ánimo y la energía.
  • Cambios cognitivos: Ligeros olvidos o dificultad para concentrarse.

A partir de los 60

  • Densidad ósea: Mayor riesgo de osteoporosis al disminuir la densidad ósea.
  • Salud cardiovascular: Aumenta el riesgo de enfermedades del corazón debido a cambios en los vasos sanguíneos y el corazón.
  • Sistema digestivo: Los cambios en la función digestiva pueden provocar problemas como el estreñimiento.
  • Salud cognitiva: Mayor riesgo de deterioro cognitivo más significativo, incluida la demencia.

Control de los síntomas del envejecimiento

Aunque el proceso de envejecimiento es natural, existen formas de controlar y mitigar estos síntomas:

  • Ejercicio regular: Ayuda a mantener la masa muscular, la salud de las articulaciones y la forma física cardiovascular.
  • Dieta equilibrada: Favorece la salud de la piel, la función metabólica y el bienestar general.
  • Salud mental: Participar en actividades cognitivas e interacciones sociales puede ayudar a mantener la agudeza mental.
  • Atención sanitaria preventiva: Cada vez es más importante someterse a revisiones periódicas.
  • Gestión del estrés: Técnicas de relajación, respiración profunda, meditación, yoga.

El envejecimiento es una parte inevitable de la vida, pero no tiene por qué mermar la calidad de vida. Comprender los plazos y síntomas típicos del envejecimiento permite una mejor preparación y una gestión proactiva. Con las estrategias adecuadas, es posible envejecer con gracia y mantener la salud y la vitalidad hasta bien entrada la vejez.

title: Obesógenos: sustancias químicas ambientales y su papel en el aumento de peso
excerpt: En los últimos años, el concepto de obesógenos (sustancias químicas ambientales que pueden contribuir al aumento de peso y la obesidad) ha ganado fuerza en la comunidad científica. ¿Qué son los obesógenos? Los obesógenos son sustancias que pueden alterar la regulación normal del metabolismo de los lípidos, lo que podría provocar un mayor almacenamiento de […]
content:
En los últimos años, el concepto de obesógenos (sustancias químicas ambientales que pueden contribuir al aumento de peso y la obesidad) ha ganado fuerza en la comunidad científica.

¿Qué son los obesógenos?

Los obesógenos son sustancias que pueden alterar la regulación normal del metabolismo de los lípidos, lo que podría provocar un mayor almacenamiento de grasa y un aumento de peso. Se encuentran en diversas fuentes, incluidos plastificantes, pesticidas y productos químicos industriales a los que los humanos estamos expuestos a diario. Estas sustancias químicas pueden alterar el equilibrio hormonal e influir en la capacidad del cuerpo para mantener su equilibrio energético.

Cómo influyen los obesógenos en el aumento de peso

Los obesógenos interfieren con una serie de vías hormonales, incluidas las que involucran el estrógeno y las hormonas tiroideas, que son cruciales para regular el metabolismo y el almacenamiento de grasa. Por ejemplo, sustancias químicas como el bisfenol A (BPA) que se encuentran en los plásticos imitan al estrógeno y pueden provocar un mayor almacenamiento de grasa. Además, algunos obesógenos pueden afectar la cantidad y el tamaño de las células grasas del cuerpo, así como las tasas metabólicas. También pueden alterar el control del apetito y el gasto energético, agravando sus efectos sobre el peso corporal.

Evidencia que vincula los obesógenos con la obesidad

Un creciente conjunto de investigaciones ha comenzado a revelar los mecanismos por los cuales los obesógenos contribuyen a la obesidad. Los estudios han demostrado que la exposición a ciertos pesticidas y plastificantes se correlaciona con un mayor índice de masa corporal y tasas de obesidad. Estos hallazgos subrayan el potencial de los obesógenos para afectar el peso corporal a través de diversas vías bioquímicas.

Minimizar la exposición a los obesógenos

Reducir la exposición a los obesógenos implica tomar decisiones informadas sobre los productos que utilizamos y los alimentos que comemos. Optar por productos orgánicos puede reducir la ingesta de pesticidas, mientras que evitar los envases de plástico para alimentos y bebidas, especialmente aquellos que contienen BPA, puede disminuir la exposición a sustancias químicas nocivas. Además, abogar por regulaciones más estrictas sobre los productos químicos industriales puede ayudar a reducir la exposición general a los obesógenos.

La conexión entre los obesógenos y el aumento de peso presenta implicaciones significativas para la salud pública, lo que enfatiza la necesidad de políticas para reducir la exposición a estas sustancias químicas. Al comprender y abordar el impacto de los factores ambientales sobre la obesidad, la sociedad podrá abordar mejor este problema complejo y creciente.

Referencias

Grün, F. y Blumberg, B. (2009). Disruptores endocrinos como obesógenos. Endocrinología molecular y celular, 304(1-2), 19-29.

Janesick, A. y Blumberdr, B. (2011). Minirevisión: PPARgamma como objetivo de los obesógenos. Revista de bioquímica de esteroides y biología molecular, 127(1-2), 4-8.

Heindel, J. J. y Blumberg, B. (2019). Obesógenos ambientales: Mecanismos y controversias. Revisión anual de farmacología y toxicología, 59, 89-106.

title: Obesogens: Environmental Chemicals and Their Role in Weight Gain
excerpt: In recent years, the concept of obesogens—environmental chemicals that may contribute to weight gain and obesity—has gained traction in the scientific community. What are Obesogens? Obesogens are substances that can disrupt the normal regulation of lipid metabolism, potentially leading to increased fat storage and weight gain. They are found in various sources including plasticizers, pesticides, […]
content:
In recent years, the concept of obesogens—environmental chemicals that may contribute to weight gain and obesity—has gained traction in the scientific community.

What are Obesogens?

Obesogens are substances that can disrupt the normal regulation of lipid metabolism, potentially leading to increased fat storage and weight gain. They are found in various sources including plasticizers, pesticides, and industrial chemicals that humans are exposed to daily. These chemicals can alter hormonal balance and influence the body’s ability to maintain its energy balance.

How Obesogens Influence Weight Gain

Obesogens interfere with a number of hormonal pathways, including those involving estrogen and thyroid hormones, which are crucial for regulating metabolism and fat storage. For example, chemicals like bisphenol A (BPA) found in plastics mimic estrogen and can lead to enhanced fat storage. Furthermore, some obesogens can affect the number and size of fat cells in the body, as well as metabolic rates. They may also alter appetite control and energy expenditure, compounding their effects on body weight.

Evidence Linking Obesogens to Obesity

A growing body of research has begun to unveil the mechanisms by which obesogens contribute to obesity. Studies have shown that exposure to certain pesticides and plasticizers correlates with increased body mass index and obesity rates. These findings underscore the potential of obesogens to affect body weight through various biochemical pathways.

Minimizing Exposure to Obesogens

Reducing exposure to obesogens involves making informed choices about the products we use and the food we eat. Opting for organic produce can reduce pesticide intake, while avoiding plastic containers for food and drink, especially those containing BPA, can decrease exposure to harmful chemicals. Additionally, advocating for stricter regulations on industrial chemicals can help reduce overall exposure to obesogens.

The connection between obesogens and weight gain presents significant implications for public health, emphasizing the need for policies to reduce exposure to these chemicals. By understanding and addressing the impact of environmental factors on obesity, society can better tackle this complex and growing problem.

References

  1. Grün, F., & Blumberg, B. (2009). Endocrine disrupters as obesogens. Molecular and Cellular Endocrinology, 304(1-2), 19-29.
  2. Janesick, A., & Blumberdr, B. (2011). Minireview: PPARgamma as the target of obesogens. Journal of Steroid Biochemistry and Molecular Biology, 127(1-2), 4-8.
  3. Heindel, J. J., & Blumberg, B. (2019). Environmental obesogens: Mechanisms and controversies. Annual Review of Pharmacology and Toxicology, 59, 89-106.

title: Glicación de proteínas y envejecimiento: Comprender su papel como biomarcador
excerpt: La glicación de las proteínas, a menudo denominada reacción de Maillard, se produce cuando las moléculas de azúcar se unen espontáneamente a las proteínas sin la ayuda de enzimas. Esta reacción es responsable de la formación de productos finales de glicación avanzada (AGE), que se acumulan en el organismo con el paso del tiempo. Los […]
content:
La glicación de las proteínas, a menudo denominada reacción de Maillard, se produce cuando las moléculas de azúcar se unen espontáneamente a las proteínas sin la ayuda de enzimas. Esta reacción es responsable de la formación de productos finales de glicación avanzada (AGE), que se acumulan en el organismo con el paso del tiempo. Los AGE pueden afectar a casi todos los tipos de células y moléculas del organismo y están relacionados con varias enfermedades asociadas al envejecimiento.

¿Qué es la glicación de proteínas?

La glicación de proteínas consiste en la unión de azúcares a proteínas, formando compuestos nocivos conocidos como AGE. Estos compuestos son especialmente perjudiciales porque pueden provocar cambios estructurales y funcionales en diversos tejidos. A medida que las personas envejecen, aumenta la acumulación de AGE, lo que contribuye al daño celular y tisular característico del proceso de envejecimiento.

El impacto de la glicación en el envejecimiento

La acumulación de AGE influye significativamente en el proceso de envejecimiento. En la diabetes, los AGE contribuyen a la disfunción de la acción de la insulina y del metabolismo de la glucosa. En el sistema cardiovascular, las proteínas glicosiladas pueden endurecer los vasos sanguíneos y hacerlos más propensos a la aterosclerosis, lo que aumenta el riesgo de cardiopatías. Del mismo modo, en el cerebro, los AGE pueden acumularse y contribuir al desarrollo de enfermedades neurodegenerativas como el Alzheimer. Los riñones también sufren los efectos de la glicación, ya que puede dañar proteínas esenciales para la función renal, provocando afecciones como la nefropatía.

Evaluar la glicación como factor biológico

La hemoglobina glucosilada (HbA1c) es un biomarcador bien conocido que se utiliza para evaluar la concentración media de glucosa en sangre a lo largo de varios meses. Proporciona una medida útil del grado de glicación que se produce en el organismo y se utiliza ampliamente para controlar y diagnosticar la diabetes. Los niveles elevados de HbA1c sugieren mayores cantidades de proteínas glicosiladas, lo que indica un mayor estrés oxidativo y potencial inflamatorio en el organismo.

Estrategias para minimizar la glicación

Para minimizar la glicación y reducir la acumulación de AGE, es crucial reducir la ingesta de azúcar. Menos azúcar en la dieta significa menos sustratos disponibles para la glicación. La incorporación de antioxidantes a través de la dieta también puede ayudar a proteger los tejidos de las condiciones oxidativas que promueven la glicación. Además, la adopción de métodos de cocción que utilicen temperaturas más bajas y más humedad puede reducir la formación de AGE en los alimentos.

La relación entre la glicación de las proteínas y el envejecimiento pone de relieve la importancia del estilo de vida y de la dieta para moderar los efectos del envejecimiento. Al comprender y abordar los factores que influyen en la glicación, las personas pueden tomar medidas significativas para mejorar su salud y su longevidad.

 

References

  1. Singh, R., Barden, A., Mori, T., & Beilin, L. (2001). Advanced glycation end-products: a review. Diabetologia, 44(2), 129-146.
  2. Semba, R. D., Nicklett, E. J., & Ferrucci, L. (2010). Does accumulation of advanced glycation end products contribute to the aging phenotype? Journal of Gerontology, 65(9), 963-975.
  3. Goldin, A., Beckman, J. A., Schmidt, A. M., & Creager, M. A. (2006). Advanced glycation end products: sparking the development of diabetic vascular injury. Circulation, 114(6), 597-605.

title: How IV Therapy Can Boost Your Metabolism and Help You Lose Weight
excerpt: You got your period earlier this week. You’ve been killing your diet and weight-loss goals, and your appetite has been in check. A few weeks later, your appetite for carbs is inconsolable. You have trouble regulating your mood, and you want to eat food for comfort. Next thing you know, you’re up 6 pounds on […]
content:
You got your period earlier this week. You’ve been killing your diet and weight-loss goals, and your appetite has been in check.

A few weeks later, your appetite for carbs is inconsolable. You have trouble regulating your mood, and you want to eat food for comfort.

Next thing you know, you’re up 6 pounds on the scale. This happens every month, a cycle of weight gain and weight loss, seemingly out of your control.

If this is you, and you wish to break this cycle and finally lose the weight, you may want to consider IV therapy.

Read on to learn how intravenous therapy can increase your metabolism and bolster your weight loss efforts.

What is IV Therapy?

Through IV therapy, a medical professional delivers essential fluids, nutrients, and medications directly to your veins. This can be used to treat chronic dehydration to more complex diseases like fibromyalgia.

In its most basic form, the doctor will insert a needle into your vein, connected to external tubing. This setup often includes a “cannula,” so multiple IV therapies can be delivered through the same IV drip.

Parenteral Nutrition

This is the act of delivering nutrients to a patient through an intravenous line.

The solution may contain any of the following:

  • Salts
  • Dextrose
  • Lipids
  • Vitamins
  • Amino Acids

The solution’s contents should be adjusted to the patient’s needs.

Benefits of IV Therapy

Any fitness coach will tell you that you can’t exercise off a bad diet. What you can do is supplement your existing diet to ensure you are getting the nutrients you need for optimal bodily function.

IV therapy can help with:

  • Stress levels
  • Hangovers
  • Cold and flu recovery
  • Skin, hair, and nail health
  • Immune system supplementation
  • Boosting energy
  • Pre-and-post surgical operations

The benefit of IV therapy is that nutrients are delivered straight to the bloodstream, bypassing the body’s natural filters. For patients that have gastrointestinal issues preventing nutrient absorption, IV administration is ideal.

You’ll want to work with a trained medical professional to ensure proper hygiene standards in a safe and sterile environment.

Alternative Weight Loss Ideas

IV therapy should sit high on your list of alternative weight loss ideas; it could be the boost you need. If you are suffering from food sensitivities, IBS, or PCOS, you may want to look into intravenous nutrient delivery.

Often, patients looking to lose weight go on fairly restrictive diets. As a result, they cut calories, but many also cut essential nutrients the body needs.

If the body senses it is deficient in these nutrients, it may actually curb its metabolism and stall weight loss.

In this case, the benefits of IV therapy could be manifold, meaning it could help you lose weight through several different mechanisms.

Stress Reduction

Increased cortisol levels are associated with higher weight outcomes.

We get stressed, and we want to eat.

IV therapy drips can help reduce stress levels, improve cognitive function (to help you make better diet decisions), and increase metabolism.

This will help with weight management in the long run.

Protein

Higher levels of lean muscle in the body are associated with increased metabolism.

In order for the body to build strong muscles, you need to be getting the proper amino acids (the building blocks of protein). Some of these cannot be synthesized in the human body, and are considered to be “essential amino acids.”

There are 9 essential amino acids: histidine, leucine, tryptophan, lysine, isoleucine, methionine, phenylalanine, valine, and threonine.

If you are on a restrictive diet for weight loss, there is a chance you are not eating all the necessary amino acids. These can be delivered to your body through IV therapy.

Better Sleep and More Energy

IV therapy can improve weight loss outcomes through several more mechanisms.

For one, it can improve your sleep. Proper rest is essential for weight loss because it regulates the hunger hormones ghrelin and leptin.

If you’ve ever pulled an all-nighter and experienced a bottomless appetite the next day, you can blame the dysregulation of ghrelin and leptin.

Say you have been experiencing sleep disturbances thanks to a bad cold or flu. IV therapy can boost your immune system to help you get the rest you need, and feel better faster. This will also help with weight loss by regulating your appetite through proper rest.

Another outcome is more energy; if you have more energy, you’ll be more active. You’ll probably have a higher Total Daily Energy Expenditure (TDEE), leading to more calories burned and more weight lost.

IV Therapy for Weight Loss

Clinicians won’t be injecting magic weight-loss juice into your veins, but they will be supplementing your body with the nutrients it needs to function at its best. This may be a combination of hydrating fluids, essential vitamins, or lipotropics (fat loss supplements).

Outcomes like lowered stress, increased energy, and boosted concentration all factor into weight loss success.

After all, you need the energy to be more active. You need to lower stress levels to make good diet decisions. You need proper rest and metabolic health to regulate your appetite.

IV therapy can help with all of these factors, which is why it is a great holistic cotherapy for weight loss. You’ll still need to exercise, eat healthily, and be active, but the therapy will ensure you can breeze through these things.

Supplements for Weight Loss Success

IV therapy can be a great adjunct treatment along with your weight loss regimen. Our intravenous therapy sessions generally take 20-30 minutes, and you can receive a discount with this code.

Lipotropics can help speed up your metabolism, and a customized formula of vitamins and minerals will keep your body in shape.

Consult with your primary care physician before trying any new vitamins, exercise regimens, and IV therapies.

title: Men Menopause: Aging-Related Hormone Changes in Men
excerpt: Maybe there’s a reason the word “men” is in “menopause.” Hear us out: men menopause. As men age, they may experience “andropause,” or biochemical testosterone deficiency. The older you are, the more […]
content:
Maybe there’s a reason the word “men” is in “menopause.”

Hear us out: men menopause. This phenomenon does not happen to all men, but age-related hormone changes are clinically significant for 20% of men over 60 years old.

As men age, they may experience “andropause,” or biochemical testosterone deficiency. The older you are, the more likely this deficiency will be a prevalent concern. As a result, older men may experience a lack of energy, loss of libido, frailty, and reduced change.

To ameliorate these symptoms, patients may consider testosterone replacement or bioidentical hormone replacement therapy.

Keep reading to learn whether these treatments may be right for you.

What is Andropause?

“Andropause” may refer to any of the following:

  • Testosterone deficiency
  • Androgen deficiency
  • Late-onset hypogonadism

These deficiencies may cause a cluster of symptoms in males that decrease their quality of life. You have andropause if you are experiencing:

  • Low libido
  • Decreased spontaneous erections
  • Infertility
  • Height loss
  • Hot flushes
  • Erectile dysfunction

These are either caused by or associated with a drop in testosterone production in males 50 years or older. Their prevalence increases with age.

Testosterone Deficiency and Its Effects
Low testosterone is referred to as male hypogonadism.

The testes produce insufficient levels of testosterone or the male sex hormone.

This hormone is responsible for maintaining and regulating:

  • Sexual dimorphism
  • Lean muscle mass
  • Bone density
  • Well-being and mood
  • Sexual function

Adequate testosterone levels are essential for men who want to look and feel their best.

Causes of Andropause

It’s difficult to tell what may cause andropause because testosterone levels vary depending on a man’s body mass index (BMI), nutrition, and medical history.

However, research has definitively shown that as men age past 30, they experience about a 1% drop in testosterone per year.

Drops in testosterone are also associated with:

  • Metabolic disorders
  • Medications
  • Alcohol abuse
  • Kidney failure
  • Inflammatory conditions
  • Obesity
  • Obstructive sleep apnea

If you are experiencing any of the above, be sure to get your testosterone levels checked as well. Many men who experience low testosterone have no overt symptoms, but treating the condition may greatly improve their quality of life.

Therapy

For men who want to improve their sexual function, the American College of Physicians recommends testosterone treatment.

This treatment is available as testosterone replacement and bioidentical hormone replacement therapy.

One option for men is gonadorelin acetate supplementation. This artificial hormone can prevent testes shrinkage in men, and it is associated with increased libido and sperm levels.

The type of hormone you supplement depends on the symptoms you are experiencing. If you are suffering from muscle shrinkage and weakness, you could consider something like ipamorelin, which stimulates the production of human growth hormone.

Andropause: Address Men Menopause With a Specialist Today

If you believe you may be experiencing declining testosterone levels with age and its associated symptoms, know that there are many treatment options.

Men menopause is a serious clinical issue for some patients, and as we learn more about hormones and their role in the human body, we will be better equipped to treat many health issues associated with aging.

Want to know more? Request a consultation with us today to learn more about therapeutic options.

Important: Testosterone levels may change with age and can affect multiple aspects of health. Testosterone therapy is appropriate only for selected patients following clinical evaluation, has potential risks and side effects, and requires ongoing medical monitoring. Prescription treatment is provided only when medically appropriate, and individual results vary.

title: Los 5 Secretos Para Una Vida Larga Y Sana
excerpt: Basados en observaciones de poblaciones longevas y en estudios de laboratorio existen intervenciones que pueden prolongar la vida, o al menos asegurar una vejez sana. El envejecimiento sano se refiere a aumentar nuestra edad con un mínimo de perdida de nuestras facultades físicas y mentales. 1- Limitar las calorías que comemos: En la medida […]
content:
Basados en observaciones de poblaciones longevas y en estudios de laboratorio existen intervenciones que pueden prolongar la vida, o al menos asegurar una vejez sana. El envejecimiento sano se refiere a aumentar nuestra edad con un mínimo de perdida de nuestras facultades físicas y mentales.

1- Limitar las calorías que comemos: En la medida que envejecemos nuestro requerimiento de calorías también disminuye. Las personas longevas tiendes a comer pequeñas porciones. Estudios de laboratorio también han demostrado que animales a los que se le limita el consumo de calorías en 30% viven un promedio de 30% más de vida.

2- Mantenerse físicamente activo: Esto no necesariamente quiere decir ir a un gimnasio, pero mantenerse activo durante la mayor parte del día. Caminar frecuentemente, usar las escaleras y parquear lejos para tener que caminar. Aun en la oficia, si usamos un stand-up desk (buro que se puede levantar para trabajar parados) podemos gastar hasta 500 calorías más durante el día de trabajo.

3- Mantenerse activo en el núcleo familiar y la comunidad. Varios estudios demográficos han demostrado que las personas mayores que se mantienen en contacto constante con amigos y familiares viven varios años más. A veces tan simple como cocinar para todos una vez a la semana da un sentido de propósito mientras envejecemos.

4- Comer sobre todo verduras y vegetales. Aunque controversial (y no me refiero a ser vegetarianos), el comer mayormente verduras, vegetales, frutas, que sean el 70 a 80% de nuestra comida diaria ha mostrado mejorar marcadores de inflamación que se pueden asociar con una vejez más sana.

5- Reponer los nutrientes y hormonas que van decayendo con la edad. Después de los 40 años nuestra capacidad de extraer nutrientes de las comidas (además de la calidad cada vez peor de la calidad del suelo y los alimentos) puede traer desnutrición. También nuestra producción de hormonas decae con la edad. En ocasiones es necesario suplementar esos nutrientes/vitaminas y hormonas para preservar nuestras funciones físicas y mentales.

Por un Envejecimiento Saludable,

Dr. Adonis.

title: How Long Does HRT Take to Work? A Realistic Timeline
metaTitle: How Long Does HRT Take to Work? A Realistic Timeline | Dr. Adonis
metaDescription: Wondering how long HRT takes to work? See the real week-by-week timeline for hormone therapy relief, symptom by symptom, from Dr. Adonis in Miami, FL.
excerpt: Most people notice small changes within 2 to 4 weeks of starting HRT, with stronger relief by 6 to 12 weeks and full benefits by 3 to 6 months. Here is the real timeline, symptom by symptom, and when to speak up if nothing has shifted.
content:
Most people notice small changes within 2 to 4 weeks of starting HRT, with stronger relief by 6 to 12 weeks and full benefits by 3 to 6 months.

How fast you feel a difference depends on which symptoms you're treating, the type of hormone therapy you use, and your dose.

If nothing has shifted by 8 to 12 weeks, it usually means your protocol needs adjusting, not that HRT isn't working for you.

You started HRT hoping to feel like yourself again, and two weeks in, nothing much has changed.

That gap between starting treatment and actually feeling different is the part almost nobody explains clearly.

How long does HRT take to work?

Long enough that patience matters, but not so long that you should sit quietly through months of no improvement.

Here is the real timeline, broken down by symptom and by treatment type, so you know what to expect and when to speak up.

GET HELP BALANCING YOUR HORMONES

How Long Does HRT Take to Work?

Most people notice small changes within 2 to 4 weeks of starting hormone replacement therapy.

Stronger relief usually builds by 6 to 12 weeks, and the NHS puts full symptom relief at up to three months for most people.

Some symptoms ease faster than others, so a flat timeline never tells the whole story.

That range is wide on purpose.

Hormone levels don't jump straight from low to optimal the moment you take your first dose or apply your first patch.

They rise gradually, and your body needs time to respond to that rise.

Two people starting the exact same protocol can feel different at the exact same point in treatment.

Dose, hormone type, delivery method, and which symptoms bother you most all change how fast relief shows up.

GET THE MOST OUT OF YOUR HRT TREATMENT

Why HRT Doesn't Work Overnight

Hormones don't act like a light switch.

They act more like a thermostat resetting itself, and that reset takes repeated signal, not a single dose.

Estrogen affects a part of your brain called the hypothalamus, which controls body temperature and plays a role in hot flashes and night sweats.

Researchers believe estrogen works there partly through a signaling pathway that needs steady, sustained hormone exposure to recalibrate.

That's one reason bioidentical hormone replacement therapy is built around consistent, structurally identical hormones instead of a single large dose.

There's also real variability between people.

Research on hormone therapy pharmacology has found that estrogen levels in your body don't reliably track with the dose on your prescription, which is part of why two people on identical doses can end up feeling different at different speeds.

Your Week-by-Week HRT Timeline

No two timelines look identical, but most people move through a similar shape.

Here's what tends to happen, stage by stage.

Weeks 1 to 2

Most people notice very little in the first two weeks.

Hormone levels are still rising, and your body hasn't had enough sustained exposure to shift symptoms yet.

Some people notice slightly better sleep or a calmer mood in this window.

Feeling nothing yet is normal and doesn't mean your protocol is wrong.

Weeks 3 to 6

This is usually when hot flashes and night sweats start to ease.

They may not disappear, but they often become less frequent or less intense.

Mood can also start to stabilize here, though this varies more than hot flash relief does.

Weeks 8 to 12

By this point, most people feel a real, noticeable difference.

Sleep is more consistent, hot flashes have usually settled, and day-to-day mood feels steadier.

This is also the point where your provider will typically check labs again and adjust your dose if your symptoms and numbers don't line up.

Months 3 to 6

The slower-moving symptoms, like vaginal dryness, libido, and changes in body composition, usually need this much time to shift meaningfully.

If you're wondering whether it makes sense to keep going once you feel better, that decision is personal and worth revisiting with your provider instead of assuming hormone therapy has a built-in expiration date.

How Long After Starting HRT Do You Feel a Difference?

Most people feel a subtle difference within 2 to 4 weeks, most often better sleep or a slightly calmer mood.

A clearer, more obvious difference tends to show up by 6 to 8 weeks, once hot flashes and night sweats have had time to ease.

If you feel nothing at all by 8 weeks, that's worth a conversation with your provider, not a reason to assume HRT isn't for you.

It helps to track your symptoms instead of relying on memory.

Hot flash frequency, sleep quality, and mood are all easy to underestimate week to week, and small improvements add up faster than they feel like they do in the moment.

Men starting testosterone therapy often follow a similar early pattern, noticing energy and motivation shift before strength or body composition catches up.

Which Symptoms Improve First, and Which Take Longer?

Hot flashes, night sweats, and sleep usually improve first, often within 2 to 6 weeks.

Mood and brain fog typically take a few more weeks.

Vaginal dryness, libido, and changes in body composition are the slowest to shift, often taking 3 to 6 months of consistent treatment.

Hot flashes and night sweats

These are usually the fastest symptoms to respond.

Many people notice fewer, milder hot flashes within 2 to 6 weeks, with stronger relief by 8 to 12 weeks.

Sleep and mood

Sleep often improves alongside hot flash relief, since fewer night sweats mean fewer wakeups.

Mood tends to follow a similar timeline, though ongoing stress or poor sleep from other causes can slow it down.

Vaginal dryness and libido

These symptoms typically move slower.

Systemic hormone therapy can take a few months to meaningfully improve vaginal tissue and libido, though local vaginal estrogen can work faster for dryness specifically.

These often overlap with the broader symptoms of low estrogen, which can also show up as joint pain, brain fog, or recurring urinary tract infections well before dryness itself becomes obvious.

Energy, weight, and body composition

These are the slowest symptoms to shift, usually taking 3 to 6 months of consistent treatment.

Hormones influence metabolism and muscle maintenance, but changes here also depend on sleep, stress, and activity level, not hormone therapy alone.

Does the Type of HRT You Use Change the Timeline?

Yes.

Transdermal patches, gels, and sprays raise hormone levels faster and more steadily than pills because they skip liver processing first.

Pellets release hormones slowly over months, so they build up gradually rather than working fast.

Men on testosterone replacement therapy often notice energy and mood shifts within 2 to 4 weeks, though body composition changes take longer.

Patches, gels, and sprays

These absorb through the skin and go straight into your bloodstream, skipping the liver on the first pass.

That tends to produce steadier hormone levels and can mean earlier symptom relief for some people.

Pills

Oral hormones pass through the liver before reaching the rest of your body.

This first-pass metabolism can delay how quickly hormone levels build and slightly changes how your body processes the dose.

Pellets and compounded doses

Pellets release hormones slowly over months, so they build up gradually rather than working fast right away.

Compounded, dose-matched preparations let your provider adjust the exact amount based on your labs rather than the nearest standard tablet strength, which can shorten how long it takes to land on the right dose for you.

What If You Don't Feel Better After 8 to 12 Weeks?

If 8 to 12 weeks pass with no real change, the most common reason is a dose or hormone type that doesn't match your labs and symptoms, not that hormone therapy doesn't work for you.

A full hormone panel, not just the one hormone you started with, usually explains why.

Hormones don't operate alone.

Estrogen, progesterone, testosterone, cortisol, and your thyroid all influence each other, and a problem in one area can blunt the results of treating another.

Correcting estrogen while an underlying thyroid issue goes unaddressed can leave you still feeling tired or foggy even though your hormone panel technically improved.

This is also where dose matters more than most people expect.

A level that falls inside a normal lab range doesn't always mean the dose is right for you personally.

Major hormone therapy guidelines call for periodic reevaluation of dose, type, and route based on how a person actually feels, not just where their labs land.

If you're past 12 weeks with no real shift, the next step usually isn't stopping hormone therapy.

It's a closer look at your full panel and an honest conversation about whether your current dose, hormone type, or delivery method actually fits your symptoms.

CONTACT US

Signs Your HRT Is Working

You'll usually know HRT is working when hot flashes and night sweats become less frequent, sleep gets more consistent, and your mood feels steadier without an obvious reason why.

Concentration and energy tend to improve gradually over the following months, alongside slower-moving changes like better skin and less joint discomfort.

  • Fewer or milder hot flashes and night sweats
  • Falling asleep more easily and staying asleep longer
  • A steadier mood, with fewer sudden swings
  • Better concentration and less brain fog
  • Gradually improving energy over several months

How Dr. Adonis Approaches Your Hormone Timeline

Your timeline should be based on your labs and your symptoms together, not a single hormone level checked in isolation.

Dr. Adonis starts with a full hormone panel, covering estrogen, progesterone, testosterone, DHEA, cortisol, and thyroid, because a slow response to treatment is often explained by one of these other hormones rather than a failure of the treatment itself.

This applies to men and women alike.

Hormonal health isn't only a women's issue, and andropause in men often gets missed for the same reason perimenopause does: symptoms build slowly and get written off as normal aging.

Doses are compounded and matched to your labs rather than the nearest standard strength, and every adjustment is reviewed by Dr. Adonis directly rather than an algorithm or a rotating prescriber.

Care is available in-office in Miami or through Florida telehealth if an in-person visit isn't practical.

If your hormone therapy timeline doesn't match what you were told to expect, or you're not sure where to start, Dr. Adonis can build a hormone panel and a protocol suited to your actual labs and symptoms, not a generic dosing chart.

SCHEDULE A CONSULTATION

FAQs: How Long Does HRT Take to Work

How long does HRT take to work for hot flashes specifically?

Hot flashes are usually one of the faster symptoms to respond to hormone therapy. Many people notice fewer or milder hot flashes within 2 to 6 weeks, with stronger relief typically settling in by 8 to 12 weeks.

How long after starting HRT do you feel a difference?

Most people feel a subtle difference within 2 to 4 weeks, often in sleep or mood first. A clearer difference tends to show up by 6 to 8 weeks as hot flashes and night sweats ease.

Is it normal to feel worse before you feel better on HRT?

Some people notice mild side effects like breast tenderness, bloating, or irregular bleeding in the first few weeks as their body adjusts to new hormone levels. This typically settles within the first one to three months and is different from HRT not working.

Does testosterone therapy work faster than estrogen therapy?

Not necessarily faster, but often noticeable in different ways. Men on testosterone replacement therapy frequently notice energy and mood changes within 2 to 4 weeks, while strength and body composition changes usually take a few months.

How long does it take for bioidentical hormone pellets to start working?

Pellets release hormones gradually, so they typically take longer to reach a steady effect than a patch or gel, often several weeks before levels build up fully. Once levels stabilize, the effect tends to stay steady until the next pellet insertion.

When should you follow up with your doctor after starting HRT?

Most providers recheck labs and symptoms around 8 to 12 weeks after starting or changing a dose. Reach out sooner if you notice concerning side effects or if symptoms haven't shifted at all by that point.

title: HRT and Hair Growth: How Hormone Therapy Affects Thinning Hair
metaTitle: HRT and Hair Growth: How Hormone Therapy Affects Thinning Hair | Dr. Adonis
metaDescription: Wondering how HRT and hair growth are connected? Learn what causes hormonal hair thinning and how bioidentical HRT may help. Book a consult with Dr. Adonis.
excerpt: Thinning hair during perimenopause and menopause is often tied to falling estrogen and rising androgen sensitivity, not just age. Hormone therapy can help slow shedding and support regrowth for some women, especially when it treats the whole hormone system instead of one number.
content:
Thinning hair during perimenopause and menopause is often tied to falling estrogen and rising androgen sensitivity, not just age.

Hormone therapy can help slow shedding and support regrowth for some women, especially when it treats the whole hormone system instead of one number.

Results typically take three to six months and work best paired with topical treatment and a root-cause evaluation.

Your hair used to hold its volume without much thought.

Now it's thinner at the part, coming out in the shower, and no shampoo switch seems to fix it.

If this started around the same time as hot flashes, irregular cycles, or brain fog, hormones are worth a serious look.

Hair growth depends on a steady supply of estrogen, balanced against androgens like testosterone and DHT.

When that balance shifts during perimenopause and menopause, hair follicles feel it before almost anything else shows up on a lab report.

This guide looks at what the research actually shows about HRT and hair growth, why hormone therapy helps some women more than others, and what actually moves the needle when hair loss and hormones overlap.

SEE IF HRT CAN HELP YOUR HAIR LOSS

How Common Is Hair Thinning During Menopause?

Hair thinning is one of the most common, and least talked about, effects of menopause.

A cross-sectional study of postmenopausal women found that 52.2 percent had some degree of female pattern hair loss, most of it mild to moderate.

That number surprises a lot of women, mainly because hair loss doesn't get the same airtime as hot flashes or night sweats.

It's easy to blame a new shampoo, stress, or getting older, when the real driver is often the same hormone shift causing everything else.

The same study found that age, time since menopause, and body weight all played a role.

That lines up with what shows up in real evaluations: hair changes rarely happen in isolation from every other hormonal symptom.

Why Does Hair Thin When Your Hormones Change?

Hair thins during perimenopause and menopause because falling estrogen shortens the hair growth phase while androgens like DHT become relatively more active, causing follicles to shrink and cycle faster.

The result is thinner strands, slower regrowth, and more visible shedding, especially along the part and temples.

Estrogen's Role in the Hair Growth Cycle

Estrogen keeps hair follicles in the anagen, or growth, phase longer.

Estrogen receptors sit directly in hair follicles, which is part of why hormone shifts show up on your scalp and not just in your mood or sleep.

When estrogen drops, hair spends less time growing and more time resting or shedding.

Strands also tend to grow back finer, since the follicle itself can shrink slightly with each cycle.

How Androgens and DHT Contribute to Thinning

Estrogen and androgens work like a seesaw.

As estrogen declines, androgens including testosterone and DHT gain more relative influence over hair follicles, even if your actual testosterone level hasn't changed much.

DHT binds to receptors in genetically sensitive follicles and gradually shrinks them, a process called miniaturization.

Over time, thick terminal hairs get replaced by shorter, finer ones, which is what creates the widening part line typical of female pattern hair loss.

Thyroid, Cortisol, and Other Hormones That Affect Hair

Estrogen and androgens aren't the only hormones involved.

An undiagnosed thyroid dysfunction is one of the most overlooked, and most fixable, causes of diffuse hair shedding in women, since thyroid hormone helps regulate the hair growth cycle directly.

Chronically high cortisol from long-term stress can push hair follicles into the resting phase early, adding another layer of shedding on top of whatever menopause is already doing.

This is exactly why treating hair loss as a single-hormone problem often falls short.

Can HRT Help Regrow Hair?

Hormone replacement therapy can help some women regrow hair by restoring estrogen levels that support the growth phase of the hair cycle, but it isn't guaranteed and results vary by individual.

The strongest evidence shows improvement in frontal hairline thinning rather than a full reversal of hair loss.

What the Research Actually Shows

One of the more detailed studies followed 11 postmenopausal women through six months of estradiol therapy.

Frontal hairline thinning improved significantly by month six, and the strength required to pluck a resting hair rose from an average of 49.7 to 63.6 grams-force, meaning hair was anchored more securely in the scalp.

That same study found no significant change in overall hair density or growth rate, which matters.

HRT appeared to strengthen and stabilize existing hair more than it generated large amounts of brand new growth.

A broader review of the hormonal transition through menopause backs this up: estrogen's protective effect on hair is real, but it interacts with genetics, age, and androgen sensitivity in ways that differ from woman to woman.

That's why two people on the same protocol can have very different results.

The formulation matters too.

Bioidentical vs. synthetic hormones behave differently in the body, which is part of why some women see better results with one type over the other.

What Determines Whether HRT Works for You

Not every woman responds to HRT the same way, and that's not random.

Genetics plays a large role, since some hair follicles are simply more sensitive to androgens than others, regardless of how much estrogen is circulating.

How soon you start treatment after menopause begins also matters.

Follicles that have been androgen-dominant for years are harder to recover than ones caught early in the transition, which is part of why addressing symptoms sooner tends to produce better hair outcomes.

The route of delivery matters too.

Oral estrogen passes through the liver first, which changes how much reaches your bloodstream compared to transdermal patches or creams, and that difference can influence how much support your hair follicles actually receive.

SEE IF HRT IS RIGHT FOR YOU

How Long Does It Take to See Results From HRT?

Most women don't notice a difference in hair for at least three months on hormone therapy, and meaningful change in thickness or shedding typically takes four to six months.

That timeline follows the hair growth cycle itself, not how quickly hormone levels normalize in your bloodstream.

Hormone levels in your blood can normalize within weeks of starting treatment, but hair doesn't work on that schedule.

A single hair follicle spends months in its growth phase before it even reaches a length where you'd notice a difference.

Shedding sometimes gets slightly worse in the first six to eight weeks before it improves, since follicles that were already primed to fall out complete that cycle regardless of new hormone support.

That temporary increase isn't a sign the treatment failed.

It's part of the hair growth cycle resetting.

Hair isn't the only thing on a longer timeline.

Many women also want to know how long they can safely stay on HRT, since hair maintenance often depends on staying consistent with treatment rather than finishing a short course.

Why HRT Alone Doesn't Always Fix Hair Loss

Hormone therapy treats one part of a bigger picture.

If an undiagnosed thyroid problem, chronic inflammation, or an iron deficiency is also feeding your hair loss, replacing estrogen alone will only get you partway there.

This is also why generic HRT protocols built around a single lab number can underperform.

Dosing that looks correct on paper doesn't always account for how progesterone, testosterone, cortisol, and thyroid hormones are interacting with each other in your specific case.

A root-cause functional medicine approach looks at the full hormone network, along with nutrient status and inflammation, before assuming estrogen replacement alone will solve hair thinning.

For some women, that broader evaluation uncovers exactly why HRT alone hadn't worked.

What Should You Combine With HRT for Hair Regrowth?

Combining hormone replacement therapy with a topical treatment like minoxidil, along with correcting any underlying nutrient or thyroid issues, generally produces better results than HRT alone.

Each addresses a different part of the hair growth cycle, so together they cover more ground than any single treatment.

Minoxidil and Topical Treatments

Minoxidil works differently than HRT.

Instead of changing your hormone levels, it widens blood vessels near the follicle and extends the growth phase directly at the scalp.

Used together, HRT addresses the hormonal environment while minoxidil supports the follicle itself.

Most people using topical minoxidil see initial results within about four months of consistent daily use, a similar timeline to hormone therapy.

Addressing the Root Cause First

Before adding another product, it's worth confirming what's actually driving the shedding.

Low iron, vitamin D deficiency, and other symptoms of low estrogen often show up together, and treating all of them tends to produce better results than treating hair on its own.

A full hormone panel, rather than a single estrogen or thyroid test, is what actually shows whether hair loss is hormonal, nutritional, or some combination of both.

How Dr. Adonis Approaches Hair Loss and Hormone Therapy

At our Miami practice, hair thinning is rarely treated as its own isolated complaint.

When a patient brings it up, it usually opens the door to a broader conversation about perimenopause, menopause, or a thyroid issue that hasn't been caught yet.

Dr. Adonis starts with a whole-system hormone panel rather than testing estrogen alone, since androgens, thyroid hormones, and cortisol all influence how hair responds to treatment.

From there, bioidentical hormone replacement therapy is dosed against your labs and symptoms together, not matched to the nearest standard prescription strength.

Florida residents can complete labs locally and manage most of the process through telehealth, with Dr. Adonis Maiquez overseeing every panel and dosing decision personally rather than handing it off to a rotating prescriber.

Thinning hair during perimenopause or menopause is frustrating, but it's rarely as simple as bad luck or getting older.

When it's tied to a real, measurable hormone shift, hair is often one of the first signs that something bigger is worth addressing.

If you're noticing hair changes alongside hot flashes, sleep problems, or mood swings, a full hormone panel can show whether HRT and hair growth are connected in your specific case.

Dr. Adonis Maiquez works with patients across Florida to book a hormone consultation and build a protocol around your actual labs and symptoms, not just one number on a page.

SCHEDULE A CONSULTATION

FAQs: HRT and Hair Growth

Does HRT help with hair loss during menopause?

For many women, yes. Restoring estrogen can help slow shedding and support thicker regrowth, especially around the frontal hairline, though results vary and HRT isn't guaranteed to reverse hair loss completely.

Can HRT make hair loss worse?

In some cases, yes. Formulations that include testosterone or synthetic progestins can increase androgen activity in certain women, which may worsen thinning instead of improving it. This is one reason hormone type and dose matter as much as simply starting treatment.

How long does it take for HRT to help with hair growth?

Most women need at least three months before noticing any change, with more meaningful improvement in hair thickness and shedding showing up around four to six months. Hair growth follows its own biological cycle, so results take longer to appear than changes in mood or sleep.

Should I combine HRT with minoxidil?

Combining the two often works better than either treatment alone, since HRT addresses the hormonal environment while minoxidil supports the follicle directly at the scalp. Many women use both together under medical supervision for a more complete approach.

Does testosterone in HRT affect hair growth?

It can go either way. Some women tolerate testosterone in their HRT protocol without any hair effects, while others are more sensitive to its conversion into DHT, which can contribute to thinning. This is part of why dosing should be individualized rather than standardized.

Do I need a full hormone panel before starting HRT for hair loss?

Yes, a full panel is important because estrogen is rarely the only hormone involved in hair thinning. Testing progesterone, testosterone, thyroid hormones, and cortisol together gives a clearer picture of what's actually driving the shedding before starting treatment.
